summary.text: A pair-word encoding of the run-length recursion yields auxiliary sequences with exact linear recurrences, from which one proves the quasi-submultiplicative bound \(p_{m+n}\le 16p_mp_n\) and the comparison \(2p_{n-11}\le a(n)\le17664p_{n-11}\). Hence \(\log(16p_n)\) is subadditive, so Fekete’s lemma gives convergence of \(\log p_n/n\); the comparison squeezes \(\log a(n)/n\) to the same limit, and exponentiation gives the desired root limit.

full_proof.text:
Let \(T_n\) denote the \(n\)-th row of A381587, indexed from 1. Thus
\[
T_1=(1),\qquad T_2=(1),\qquad T_3=(2),
\]
and, for \(n\geq 3\),
\[
T_{n+1}=\operatorname{Runs}(T_n^{\rm rev})\,T_n. \tag{1}
\]
Here juxtaposition means concatenation, “rev” means reversal, and \(\operatorname{Runs}(W)\) is the list of lengths of the consecutive constant runs of the word \(W\). Put
\[
a_n=\sum T_n.
\]
We prove that \(a_n^{1/n}\) has a limit.

The proof has two parts. The first is a combinatorial analysis of the rows which produces an auxiliary sequence \(p_k\). The second proves that \(p_k\) has a well-defined exponential growth rate and transfers that rate to \(a_n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. A pair-word dynamical system
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For a finite list of pairs
\[
P=((m_1,\ell_1),\ldots,(m_s,\ell_s))
\]
of nonnegative integers, define its binary expansion by
\[
\mathcal L(P)=A^{m_1}B^{\ell_1}\cdots A^{m_s}B^{\ell_s}. \tag{2}
\]
Define three statistics
\[
|P|_*=\sum_{i=1}^s(m_i+\ell_i),\qquad
|P|_A=\sum_{i=1}^s m_i,
\qquad \#P=s. \tag{3}
\]
Thus \(|P|_*\) is the length of \(\mathcal L(P)\).

We need the following operation on lists of positive integers. Define \(C(u)\), a list of pairs, recursively by
\[
C(())=(),
\]
and, if \(u=(x)u'\), by
\[
C((x)u')=
\begin{cases}
((m+1,\ell))R,&x=1\text{ and }C(u')=((m,\ell))R,\\
((1,0)),&x=1\text{ and }u'=(),\\
((1,x)),&x\ne1\text{ and }u'=(),\\
((1,x-1))C(u'),&x\ne1\text{ and }u'\ne().
\end{cases} \tag{4}
\]
(The second line is exactly the empty-output case in the first line.)

If \(P\) is nonempty and its last pair is \((m,\ell)\), define
\[
\Phi(P)=P^-\,((m,\ell-1))\,C((m_s,m_{s-1},\ldots,m_1)), \tag{5}
\]
where \(P^-\) is \(P\) with its last pair removed. All applications below have \(\ell\ge2\), so the decremented entry remains positive.

Start with
\[
P_0=((3,1),(1,3)),\qquad P_{k+1}=\Phi(P_k), \tag{6}
\]
and set
\[
p_k=|P_k|_*,\qquad r_k=|P_k|_A,\qquad q_k=\#P_k. \tag{7}
\]
We shall establish
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{k+1}&=p_k+r_k,\\
r_{k+1}&=r_k+q_k,\\
q_{k+5}&=q_{k+4}+p_k.
\end{aligned} \tag{8}
\]

We now give the word argument behind these identities and behind the connection with the rows \(T_n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The renormalization identity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For a list \(M=(m_1,\ldots,m_s)\), define a binary “derived-letter” word \(D(M)\) as follows. At position \(i\), emit no letter if \(m_i=1\). If \(m_i\ge2\), emit one letter, which is \(A\) precisely when the following entry is 1, and is \(B\) otherwise; at the last position “there is no following entry,” so the emitted letter there is \(B\). Thus
\[
D(M)_i=
\begin{cases}
\text{nothing},&m_i=1,\\
A,&m_i\ge2\text{ and }m_{i+1}=1,\\
B,&m_i\ge2\text{ and }(i=s\text{ or }m_{i+1}\ne1).
\end{cases} \tag{9}
\]

The key renormalization formula is
\[
D((P_{k+4})_A)=\mathcal L(P_k), \tag{10}
\]
where \((P)_A\) denotes the list of first coordinates of the pairs of \(P\).

For completeness, we prove the finite-word identities which imply (10). Say that a pair word \(P\) is admissible if:

* it begins \(((m_1,\ell_1),(1,\ell_2),\ldots)\) with \(m_1\ge2\);
* every coordinate of every pair is positive;
* its final second coordinate is at least 2.

Call it strongly admissible if, in addition, the two coordinates of its final pair are both at least 2.

First, direct use of (4) shows that if \(P\) is admissible, then \(\Phi(P)\) is strongly admissible. Indeed, the reversed first-coordinate list ends in \((1,m_1)\). An induction through (4) shows that every pair in
\(C(u(1,m_1))\) has positive coordinates and that its last pair is \((c,m_1)\) with \(c\ge2\). The old last second coordinate is merely decreased by 1 and hence stays positive. The initial pattern is unchanged unless the original word had only its two initial pairs; in that exceptional case the same pattern follows by writing (5) out directly. This also proves that every \(P_k\) is admissible and every \(P_k\), \(k\ge1\), is strongly admissible.

Next we prove the commutation identity
\[
D(P_A)=\mathcal L(Q)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
D((\Phi P)_A)=\mathcal L(\Phi Q), \tag{11}
\]
whenever \(P\) is strongly admissible and \(Q\) is admissible.

Here is a detailed derivation. Parse the reversed first-coordinate list of \(P\) into blocks
\[
Y=v_1,1^{c_1},v_2,1^{c_2},\ldots,v_t,1^{c_t}, \tag{12}
\]
where each \(v_i\ge2\). Strong admissibility at the end of \(P\), together with the initial form of \(P\), ensures that this parse is nonempty and that \(c_t=0\). A direct induction on the blocks in (12), using (4), gives
\[
(C(Y))_A=(1,c_1+1,c_2+1,\ldots,c_{t-1}+1). \tag{13}
\]
Define the binary word \(b=(b_1,\ldots,b_{t-1})\) by \(b_i=A\) if \(c_i\ge1\), and \(b_i=B\) if \(c_i=0\). Scanning (12) from right to left in the definition (9) shows
\[
\mathcal L(Q)^{\rm rev}=B b. \tag{14}
\]
The point is that each \(v_i\ge2\) emits one letter, and it emits \(A\) exactly when it is followed, in the original direction, by at least one 1.

For a binary word \(w\), let \(\Psi(w)\) be obtained by looking at every occurrence of \(A\), emitting \(A\) when the next letter is \(B\), and emitting \(B\) when the next letter is \(A\); an \(A\) at the end emits \(B\), while occurrences of \(B\) emit nothing. Formula (13), followed by the definition of \(D\), says that the newly appended part of \(D((\Phi P)_A)\) is
\[
A\Psi(b). \tag{15}
\]
The old part is \(D(P_A)\) with its last letter removed, because the final first coordinate of \(P\), which is at least 2, acquires the newly appended first coordinate 1 as its look-ahead. Therefore
\[
D((\Phi P)_A)=\mathcal L(Q)^-\,A\Psi(b), \tag{16}
\]
where the superscript \(-\) here means deletion of the final binary letter.

On the other hand, the positivity of the coordinates of \(Q\) implies that the lengths of the \(A\)-runs in \(\mathcal L(Q)^{\rm rev}\) are exactly the reversed first-coordinate list \((Q_A)^{\rm rev}\). Since \(Q\) begins with at least two \(A\)'s, (14) also implies that \(b\) ends in \(AA\). An induction on the length of such a word \(b\) gives the elementary identity
\[
\mathcal L\bigl(C(\text{lengths of the }A\text{-runs of }b)\bigr)
   =A\Psi(b). \tag{17}
\]
To see all cases in this induction: a leading \(B\) contributes no \(A\)-run and is simply deleted; a leading \(AB\) creates a new run of length 1, corresponding to the first alternative in (4); and a leading \(AA\) increases the first run length. In the last case, if that run has length 1 before the increase, the first pair in (4) is merged by increasing its first coordinate; if its length is at least 2, its second coordinate increases by one. These are precisely the two possible outputs of \(\Psi\). The terminal condition \(AA\) supplies the base case and prevents an unmatched final run.

Finally, (5) says
\[
\mathcal L(\Phi Q)=\mathcal L(Q)^-\,
 \mathcal L(C((Q_A)^{\rm rev})).
\]
Combining this with (17), (14), and (16) proves (11).

It remains only to initialize (10). Direct expansion of (4) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_0={}&((3,1),(1,3)),\\
P_1={}&((3,1),(1,2),(2,3)),\\
P_2={}&((3,1),(1,2),(2,2),(1,1),(2,3)),\\
P_3={}&((3,1),(1,2),(2,2),(1,1),(2,2),(1,1),(2,1),(2,3)),\\
P_4={}&((3,1),(1,2),(2,2),(1,1),(2,2),(1,1),(2,1),(2,2),
(1,1),(1,1),(2,1),(2,1),(2,3)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Applying (9) to the first coordinates of \(P_4\) gives
\(A^3BA B^3=\mathcal L(P_0)\). Thus (10) holds for \(k=0\). Applying (11) inductively, with \(P=P_{k+4}\) and \(Q=P_k\), proves (10) for every \(k\).

We can now count. An induction in (4) gives, for every reversed first-coordinate list occurring here,
\[
|C(P_A^{\rm rev})|_A=\#P,\qquad
|C(P_A^{\rm rev})|_*=|P|_A+1,
\]
with the extra 1 exactly compensating for the decrement of the old last second coordinate in (5). More explicitly, (4) has the following three immediate counting consequences:
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\Phi(P)|_*&=|P|_*+|P|_A,\\
|\Phi(P)|_A&=|P|_A+\#P,\\
\#\Phi(P)&=\#P+|D(P_A)|.
\end{aligned} \tag{18}
\]
For the last formula, each entry of \(P_A\) which is at least 2 contributes exactly one new pair under (4), and these are exactly the entries which emit a letter under \(D\). Applying (18) to \(P_k\), and using (10) and \(|\mathcal L(P_k)|=p_k\), proves all three recurrences (8).

The initial values, read from \(P_0\), are
\[
p_0=8,
\qquad r_0=4,
\qquad q_0=2. \tag{19}
\]
In particular all three sequences are nondecreasing, and
\[
p_k\ge8,
\qquad r_k\ge4,
\qquad q_k\ge2. \tag{20}
\]
Also, directly from their definitions and positivity of pair coordinates,
\[
r_k\le p_k,
\qquad q_k\le p_k. \tag{21}
\]
Consequently
\[
p_{k+1}=p_k+r_k\le2p_k,
\qquad p_{m+i}\le2^i p_m. \tag{22}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Connecting the pair words to the run-length rows
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We next prove the bridge from \(P_k\) to \(T_n\).

For an ordinary numerical word \(W\), let \(\operatorname{RLE}(W)\) be its run-length encoding as pairs \((\text{value},\text{multiplicity})\). Thus the list of second coordinates of \(\operatorname{RLE}(W)\) is \(\operatorname{Runs}(W)\). For a list of pairs \(Q=((v_i,c_i))\), define
\[
Z(Q)=((v_1,1),(1,c_1),\ldots,(v_s,1),(1,c_s)). \tag{23}
\]
Also define the binary shadow of a numerical word by
\[
\operatorname{sh}(x_1,\ldots,x_s)
=(\,[x_1\ge2],\ldots,[x_s\ge2] \,), \tag{24}
\]
where true is identified with \(A\) and false with \(B\).

We claim that for every \(n\ge10\) there is a pair list \(Q_n\) such that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{RLE}(T_n^{\rm rev})&=Z(Q_n),\\
&v\ne1\text{ and }c\ge1\quad\text{for every }(v,c)\in Q_n,\\
\operatorname{sh}((Q_n)_2)&=\mathcal L(P_{n-9}),
\end{aligned} \tag{25}
\]
where \((Q_n)_2\) denotes the list of second coordinates.

The base case is a direct finite expansion of the row recurrence. Successively applying (1) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{10}={}&(1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,\\
&1,1,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,2).
\end{aligned} \tag{26}
\]
Its reversed run encoding has the form (23) with
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_{10}=(& (2,3),(3,3),(3,3),(3,1),(3,5),(3,1),\\
       &(3,1),(3,7),(5,3),(3,1),(3,1),(3,1)).
\end{aligned} \tag{27}
\]
All first coordinates in (27) differ from 1, all second coordinates are positive, and their shadow is
\[
A^3BA B^3=\mathcal L(P_1),
\]
so (25) holds at \(n=10\).

We describe the induction step in full. Suppose (25) holds for \(Q_n\). Because every admissible \(P_{n-9}\) ends in at least two \(B\)'s, the final letter of \(\mathcal L(P_{n-9})\) is \(B\). Hence the final second coordinate of \(Q_n\) is 1. Write
\[
Q_n=Q'((z,1)). \tag{28}
\]
By (1), reversal, and the fact that the run lengths are the second coordinates in a run encoding,
\[
T_{n+1}^{\rm rev}
=T_n^{\rm rev}\,E(1,(Q'_2)^{\rm rev}), \tag{29}
\]
where
\[
E(x_1,\ldots,x_t)=(x_1,1,x_2,1,\ldots,x_t,1). \tag{30}
\]

The run encoding of the appended word (30) is easy to determine recursively. Let \(j\) be the number of initial 1's in a numerical word \(u\). Scanning \(E(u)\), every entry \(x\ne1\) produces a pair
\((x,2j+1)\), where \(j\) is the number of 1's immediately following it in the appropriate recursive tail; initial 1's produce one initial run \((1,2j)\). Denote the resulting list of non-1 pairs by \(S(u)\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{RLE}(E(u))=
\begin{cases}
((1,2j))Z(S(u)),&j>0,\\
Z(S(u)),&j=0.
\end{cases} \tag{31}
\]
This follows by induction on \(u\): if its first entry is 1, the two adjacent 1's in (30) enlarge the initial 1-run by 2; if it is not 1, they start a run of that value of odd length, followed by the separator 1-run.

Applying (31) to (29), the initial 1-run of the appended part merges with the final \((1,1)\) in \(Z(Q_n)\). We therefore obtain
\[
Q_{n+1}=Q'\,((z,1+2(j+1)))\,S((Q'_2)^{\rm rev}). \tag{32}
\]
Every first coordinate in the new suffix differs from 1 and every second coordinate is positive, by (31), so the positivity part of (25) is preserved.

It remains to check the shadow. If
\[
\mathcal L(P_{n-9})^{\rm rev}=B b,
\]
then (28) and (25) give
\[
b=\operatorname{sh}((Q'_2)^{\rm rev}).
\]
The middle multiplicity \(1+2(j+1)\) in (32) has true shadow \(A\). The recursive description (31) shows, by induction on the entries of \((Q'_2)^{\rm rev}\), that
\[
\operatorname{sh}(S((Q'_2)^{\rm rev})_2)=\Psi(b). \tag{33}
\]
Indeed an entry 1 emits no pair with second coordinate at least 2, whereas an entry at least 2 emits such a pair exactly when the previous shadow letter is false, which is precisely the definition of \(\Psi\).

The unchanged prefix \(Q'\) contributes \(\mathcal L(P_{n-9})\) with its final \(B\) deleted. Therefore (32) and (33) give
\[
\operatorname{sh}((Q_{n+1})_2)
=\mathcal L(P_{n-9})^- A\Psi(b).
\]
By the word identity (17), this is exactly
\(\mathcal L(\Phi(P_{n-9}))=\mathcal L(P_{n+1-9})\). This completes the induction and proves (25).

We now extract two simple row recurrences. The number of runs of \(T_n^{\rm rev}\) is, by (23), \(2\#Q_n\). By the last line of (25),
\[
\#Q_n=|\mathcal L(P_{n-9})|=p_{n-9}.
\]
Thus (1) gives, for \(n\ge10\),
\[
|T_{n+1}|=|T_n|+2p_{n-9}. \tag{34}
\]
Also the sum of all run lengths of a word is its length. Therefore, for every \(n\ge3\),
\[
a_{n+1}=|T_n|+a_n. \tag{35}
\]

Put
\[
\lambda_j=|T_{j+10}|,
\qquad \alpha_j=a_{j+10}.
\]
From (26),
\[
\lambda_0=42,
\qquad \alpha_0=67, \tag{36}
\]
and (34)-(35) become
\[
\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j+2p_{j+1},
\qquad
\alpha_{j+1}=\lambda_j+\alpha_j. \tag{37}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Fixed-factor comparison between \(a_n\) and \(p_n\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We first record several consequences of (8), (20), and (22). Since
\[
q_{k+5}=q_{k+4}+p_k
\]
and \(r_{k+6}=r_{k+5}+q_{k+5}\), we have
\[
p_k\le r_{k+6}. \tag{38}
\]
Together with \(p_{k+6}\le64p_k\), this gives, for \(k\ge6\),
\[
65p_k\le64p_{k+1}. \tag{39}
\]
Indeed write \(k=j+6\). Then \(p_j\le r_{j+6}=r_k\), while \(p_k\le64p_j\); hence \(p_k\le64r_k\), and
\(65p_k\le64(p_k+r_k)=64p_{k+1}\).

For the six values \(k=0,\ldots,5\), direct use of (8), or direct expansion of the displayed pair words, gives
\[
(p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4,p_5,p_6)
=(8,12,18,27,41,63,98).
\]
These values, together with (39), imply for every \(j\ge0\)
\[
138p_j\le136p_{j+1}, \tag{40}
\]
and
\[
8970p_j\le8832p_{j+1}. \tag{41}
\]
For \(j\ge6\), each follows immediately from the stronger ratio (39); for \(0\le j<6\), substitution of the seven displayed values proves it.

We now prove by induction from (36)-(37) that
\[
2p_j\le\lambda_j\le138p_j. \tag{42}
\]
The lower bound at \(j=0\) is \(16\le42\). If it holds at \(j\), then
\(\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j+2p_{j+1}\ge2p_{j+1}\).
For the upper bound, the induction hypothesis and (40) give
\[
\lambda_{j+1}\le138p_j+2p_{j+1}
\le136p_{j+1}+2p_{j+1}=138p_{j+1}.
\]

Similarly,
\[
\alpha_j\le8832p_j. \tag{43}
\]
The case \(j=0\) is immediate from \(67\le8832\cdot8\). If it holds for \(j\), then by (37), (42), and (41),
\[
\alpha_{j+1}
\le8832p_j+138p_j
=8970p_j
\le8832p_{j+1}.
\]
Moreover (37) and the lower half of (42) give
\[
2p_j\le\lambda_j\le\alpha_{j+1}. \tag{44}
\]
Finally, using (43) at \(j+1\) and \(p_{j+1}\le2p_j\),
\[
\alpha_{j+1}\le8832p_{j+1}\le17664p_j. \tag{45}
\]
Thus, on writing \(n=j+11\), we have for every \(n\ge11\)
\[
2p_{n-11}\le a_n\le17664p_{n-11}. \tag{46}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Quasi-submultiplicativity of \(p_k\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We prove simultaneously, for all \(m,n\ge0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{m+n}&\le16p_mp_n,\\
r_{m+n}&\le16p_mr_n,\\
q_{m+n}&\le16p_mq_n.
\end{aligned} \tag{47}
\]
The proof is by strong induction on \(n\).

If \(n<6\), (22) gives
\[
p_{m+n}\le2^np_m\le32p_m.
\]
Using (20),
\[
32p_m\le16p_m p_n,
\quad
32p_m\le16p_m r_n,
\quad
32p_m\le16p_m q_n,
\]
where the latter two estimates use \(r_n\ge4\) and \(q_n\ge2\). Since \(r_{m+n},q_{m+n}\le p_{m+n}\), all three inequalities follow.

Now let \(n=n'+1\) with \(n'\ge5\), and assume all three statements for smaller second indices. The first two recurrences in (8) and the induction hypothesis give
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{m+n'+1}
 &=p_{m+n'}+r_{m+n'}\\
 &\le16p_m(p_{n'}+r_{n'})
 =16p_mp_{n'+1},\\
r_{m+n'+1}
 &=r_{m+n'}+q_{m+n'}\\
 &\le16p_m(r_{n'}+q_{n'})
 =16p_mr_{n'+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the third inequality, rewrite the delayed recurrence in (8) as
\[
q_{x+1}=q_x+p_{x-4}\qquad(x\ge4).
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_{m+n'+1}
 &=q_{m+n'}+p_{m+n'-4}\\
 &\le16p_mq_{n'}+16p_mp_{n'-4}\\
 &=16p_m(q_{n'}+p_{n'-4})
 =16p_mq_{n'+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second use of the induction hypothesis is legitimate because \(n'-4<n'+1\). This completes the strong induction and proves (47).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Existence of the exponential growth rate
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define
\[
u_n=\log(16p_n).
\]
The first inequality in (47) implies
\[
16p_{m+n}\le(16p_m)(16p_n),
\]
and therefore
\[
u_{m+n}\le u_m+u_n. \tag{48}
\]
Thus \((u_n)\) is subadditive. It is bounded below by 0, since \(p_n\ge8\). Fekete's subadditivity lemma now gives the existence of a finite real number
\[
L_0=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{u_n}{n}
   =\inf_{n\ge1}\frac{u_n}{n}. \tag{49}
\]
Since
\[
\frac{\log p_n}{n}
=\frac{u_n}{n}-\frac{\log16}{n},
\]
we also have
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log p_n}{n}=L_0. \tag{50}
\]
A fixed shift does not change this limit. More explicitly, putting \(j=n-11\),
\[
\frac{\log p_j}{j+11}
=\frac{\log p_j}{j}\cdot\frac{j}{j+11}\longrightarrow L_0,
\]
so
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log p_{n-11}}{n}=L_0. \tag{51}
\]

All quantities in (46) are positive. Taking logarithms there and dividing by \(n\) gives, for \(n\ge11\),
\[
\frac{\log2+\log p_{n-11}}{n}
\le \frac{\log a_n}{n}
\le
\frac{\log17664+\log p_{n-11}}{n}. \tag{52}
\]
By (51), both outer expressions tend to \(L_0\), because the fixed constants divided by \(n\) tend to zero. The squeeze theorem therefore yields
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log a_n}{n}=L_0. \tag{53}
\]
Finally, for all sufficiently large \(n\), \(a_n>0\), and hence
\[
a_n^{1/n}
=
\exp\!\left(\frac{\log a_n}{n}\right).
\]
Continuity of the exponential function and (53) give
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n^{1/n}=e^{L_0}.}
\]
In particular, the limit asked for in A381358 exists.
